Process overview

From creative risk to a production-ready system

An eleven-week Double Diamond process moved from understanding where creative intent gets lost to designing, testing and delivering a shared prompt workflow for animation teams.

01 · Discover

Finding where creative intent gets lost

We began by looking beyond generation speed. Interviews, workflow mapping and participatory research showed that the deeper risk appears when creative reasoning is translated into prompts, revised across tools and handed from one role to another.

Framing the opportunity

The challenge was not AI quality alone

The DNEG brief asked how AI could support animation without weakening authorship, control or visual consistency. Early synthesis reframed the challenge around unclear intent, handoff gaps and creative drift.

Interview research

Listening across five animation perspectives

Practitioners, students, independent creators and production teams revealed the same pattern: faster generation does not automatically improve control, team visibility or the ability to explain why a decision was made.

Industry exchange

Narrowing the scope to pre-production intent

Mapping DNEG’s character workflow shifted the project from asking whether AI can generate animation to asking how AI-assisted work can remain clear, controllable and transferable before production begins.

Participatory study · n=30

Measuring where creative drift feels most likely

Participants positioned fourteen production stages by AI involvement and impact on creative direction. The aggregated map made the highest-risk moments visible: interpretation, character development, mood exploration and feedback translation.

Journey mapping

The weakest moment appears after generation

The journey map exposed a steady drop in confidence from feedback to handoff. Speed can hide deviation, review often reveals it too late, and missing rationale creates rework for the next department.

02 · Define

Turning evidence into a focused design challenge

The research converged on one need: creative intent must survive generation, review and handoff. We translated that need into opportunity areas, then narrowed them into a clear problem statement and design criteria.

Opportunity areas

Five ways to keep the original vision visible

The opportunity space combined intent locking, reusable visual structure, feedback translation, decision history and actionable handoff—connecting individual creative control with team-wide traceability.

Problem definition

How might we preserve intent without slowing the work?

Success meant more than writing a better prompt. The solution had to translate intuitive direction into reusable components, keep later-stage teams aligned and reduce the overhead of repeated explanation.

03 · Develop

Exploring, structuring and testing the solution

We explored six directions, evaluated them against the research and combined the strongest ideas into PromptKit: a structured prompt frame, shared project context and a lightweight way to capture intent before it disappears.

Concept generation

Six directions across creation, handoff and review

Each concept addressed a different break in the workflow—from translating directorial feeling into parameters to making decisions reviewable, traceable and easier to reuse.

Concept selection

One shared system, built from three complementary ideas

We assessed each direction for intent fidelity, reduced rework, prototypability and production fit. Structured prompts became the core, strengthened by shared context, traceability and fast personal capture.

System model

Team depth on web, personal speed on mobile

The web workspace holds the full prompt frame, project context, review history and handoff package. The app companion captures a minimum prompt quickly, with the option to sync and complete it with the team.

Prompt frame development

Building a shared vocabulary for visual intent

Guidance from six image-generation systems was reviewed and normalised. Affinity mapping separated semantic intent from execution controls, producing a twelve-component frame organised into Content, Design and Presentation.

Technical verification

Testing what the minimum prompt must preserve

Approximately seventy controlled variants tested dependencies, omissions and correction cost. The result was a six-field minimum frame weighted by sketch fidelity, prompt execution and artist judgement.

Prototype iteration

Reducing complexity while making decisions visible

User testing moved the prototype from one overloaded screen to a guided workflow. Each round clarified ownership, added source labels and introduced review states so teams could see what had been confirmed before handoff.

04 · Deliver

A shared workflow from sketch to production handoff

The final system keeps the source image, artist decisions, AI observations, motion parameters and handoff state connected. Teams can move quickly without losing the rationale behind the work.

Workflow architecture

Analyse, direct, generate and hand off

A sketch and task goal anchor the process. PromptKit builds a structured frame, adds motion and timing, then keeps preview, component review and delivery metadata together through handoff.

Final web experience

Creative space first, production context always close

A collapsible workspace keeps navigation, project context and handoff status available without crowding the canvas. Starting from a sketch ensures every later choice can be traced back to the original visual intent.

Design principle

AI observes; the artist decides

PromptKit separates editable AI observations from approved creative choices. Uncertainty stays visible, suggestions require confirmation and the artist remains the source of truth throughout the workflow.
